explanation: From the 1920s, American stop signs were yellow octagons; the United States switched them to red in 1954. Japan uses a red downward-pointing triangle.

claims.text: In most countries the stop sign is an octagon.
Give way, no entry and speed limit signs are not octagonal.
From the 1920s, standard stop signs in the United States were yellow octagons (the first, in Detroit in 1915, was a white square).
The United States changed its stop signs to red with white letters in 1954.
Japan's stop sign is a red downward-pointing triangle.

evidence.summaryExcerpt: Wikipedia says the first stop sign was created in 1914 by Detroit police sergeant Harold "Harry" Jackson, who cut the corners off a rectangular piece of plywood, wrote "STOP" over the center, and placed it facing the street. The FHWA timeline lists 1915, the first STOP sign appears in Detroit. [...] So the "white square" detail in your query is only partly right: the sign was a white board with its corners cut [...] Wikipedia says that from 1924 to 1954, stop signs bore a red or black stop legend on a yellow field.

claimResults.note: The main clause is supported (a yellow field from 1924 to 1954). The parenthetical is not: Detroit 1914 (Wikipedia) against 1915 (FHWA), and a white board with its corners cut against a 24 by 24 inch white sign. A reported conflict fails the claim as written (§9.5.2).

claimResults.note: The summary attributes this sentence to the FHWA, which owns the MUTCD (an FHWA MUTCD page among the results), so the call counts at Tier A for it. The conflicts the summary reports concern only the Detroit origin in c3.
